title: “Should we dialyze tonight?”
note: Fictional patient. Triggers and thresholds are illustrative, drawn from the module’s cited trials; the hospital’s protocol and the attending’s judgment come first.
intro:
You are the attending nephrologist. At 21:00 the ICU resident, Dr. Tolentino, calls about Mr. Arturo Lim, 72, on day 2 after surgery for a perforated bowel, in septic shock. His creatinine has gone from 1.5 to 4.8 mg/dL. Bicarbonate is 19 mmol/L, potassium 5.4, and his oxygen need is stable. The hospital has no continuous kidney replacement therapy (CRRT); your unit can bring a portable machine and run slow, prolonged sessions in the ICU.

“His creatinine has tripled. Should we start dialysis tonight?”

n1.prompt: What do you tell Dr. Tolentino?

choices.text: No indication tonight. Write triggers for starting, and review him in the morning.
choices.feedback: Ask what the kidney can no longer do. Potassium, acid, and fluid are all still within what his body can manage. In STARRT-AKI, starting early did not improve 90-day survival, and survivors more often stayed on dialysis. Written triggers (potassium above 6.0 despite treatment, pH below 7.15, rising oxygen need with a positive balance) let the night team act without you.

choices.text: Yes. A tripled creatinine with low urine is severe AKI (acute kidney injury), and starting early clears the toxins before they build.
choices.feedback: Creatinine alone is a number, not an indication. Accelerated starts did not save lives in STARRT-AKI, caused more adverse events, and left more survivors on dialysis. About 38% of the standard arm never needed dialysis at all.
choices.then: You think again and tell Dr. Tolentino to hold off, then write the triggers in the chart.

choices.text: Not yet. Review again in 72 hours.
choices.feedback: Waiting is right, but waiting needs a ceiling and named triggers. In AKIKI 2, waiting even longer gave no more dialysis-free days and was associated with higher mortality. Decide each day.
choices.then: You add triggers and a review for tomorrow morning.

n2.scene: The night team followed the triggers. Despite insulin with dextrose, his potassium is 6.5 mmol/L with peaked T waves; pH is 7.17. He is on high-flow oxygen, his balance is 5.2 liters positive, and norepinephrine has more than doubled. The nearest CRRT center is 90 minutes away by ambulance.

choices.text: Indication met. Slow, prolonged dialysis in this ICU, with low blood flow.
choices.feedback: Potassium rising despite treatment, acidemia, and fluid flooding the lungs: these are true indications. With climbing vasopressors he is too unstable for a fast session or a 90-minute ride. Slow, prolonged therapy where he is trades speed for steadiness.
choices.then: The ICU treats the ECG changes by protocol while your nurses and technician set up the portable machine.

choices.text: Transfer him now by ambulance to the CRRT center, since continuous therapy is what KDIGO suggests for patients who are unstable.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2012 does suggest CRRT for unstable patients (2B), but the modality has to be one you can deliver. A 90-minute ride with peaked T waves and doubling vasopressors is the riskier path. Slow therapy where he is can be continuous enough.
choices.then: The ambulance cannot leave for two hours. You change the plan to slow, prolonged dialysis in the ICU.

choices.text: A standard four-hour session today, removing 3 liters.
choices.feedback: A fast session with 3 liters of fluid removal in a man on 0.28 mcg/kg/min of norepinephrine risks a severe pressure fall. The goal is steady removal, not a large removal in a short time.
choices.then: At hour 1 his mean pressure falls to 52 mmHg and the session is stopped. You rewrite the order for slow, prolonged therapy.

n3.scene: Your nurse, an ICU nurse, and your technician are at the bedside. The water and machine checks are signed.
n3.prompt: What must your written order contain?

choices.text: Indication, modality and why, who owns each task, and the stop or transfer limits.
choices.feedback: Every acute order needs those four lines, including the hourly fluid-removal goal, the pressure at which ultrafiltration stops, and how the team reaches you. The intensivist runs the resuscitation; you write the prescription; your nurse runs the machine with the ICU nurse.

choices.text: The full machine prescription: dialyzer, blood and dialysate flow, dialysate potassium, duration and the anticoagulation.
choices.feedback: That is necessary but not sufficient. Without the indication, who owns each task, an hourly fluid goal and a pressure floor, the bedside team cannot act safely without phoning you.
choices.then: You add the indication, the task division, the fluid goal and the pressure floor.

choices.feedback: “As tolerated” leaves the bedside team guessing. Write an hourly goal and the pressure at which removal stops.
choices.then: The nurse calls you to ask what “tolerated” means. You write the hourly goal and the pressure floor.

n4.scene: Your nurse calls. His mean pressure is 57 mmHg, below the floor you wrote, even after the ICU raised norepinephrine. Potassium is down to 5.6 mmol/L.

choices.text: Stop fluid removal as written, keep clearance going if pressure allows, and review with the intensivist.
choices.feedback: The floor exists so the nurse can act at once. Stopping ultrafiltration usually lets the pressure recover, and diffusive clearance of potassium and acid can continue at low blood flow. Then decide with the intensivist whether the plan still holds or transfer is needed.
choices.then: His mean pressure returns to 63 mmHg. Fluid removal restarts at a lower hourly goal an hour later.

choices.text: Keep removing fluid and ask the ICU for saline boluses to hold the pressure, since the lungs are the reason we started.
choices.feedback: Giving fluid to keep removing fluid goes in a circle. The written floor is there to be followed; stop removal and let the pressure recover.
choices.then: The pressure stays low. You stop fluid removal and it recovers to 63 mmHg.

choices.text: End the session and return the blood.
choices.feedback: Safe, but you lose the potassium and acid clearance he still needs. Stopping fluid removal alone is usually enough.
choices.then: His pressure recovers. The session restarts that evening with a lower fluid goal.

n5.scene: Mr. Lim is off norepinephrine. He passed 950 mL of urine yesterday, up from 400 the day before. His creatinine has not risen since the last session two days ago. The ICU asks when the next session is.

choices.text: Hold dialysis, look for recovery each day, and write the triggers to restart.
choices.feedback: Rising urine output and a creatinine that no longer climbs between sessions are signs of recovery. Measure a timed urine creatinine clearance if available. Dialysis that is no longer needed exposes him to the catheter, hypotension and possibly slower recovery.

choices.text: Continue sessions until his creatinine is near baseline.
choices.feedback: Creatinine falls slowly as function returns. Keep dialyzing for a number and you may slow the recovery you are waiting for. Look for recovery and write restart triggers.

choices.text: Book a tunneled catheter and a slot at your outpatient unit, since few patients this sick recover.
choices.feedback: His urine output and creatinine say he is recovering. Planning for lifelong dialysis now is premature.

end.title: Day 14
end.text: Mr. Lim needs no more dialysis. His creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL at discharge, the catheter is removed, and he is booked at the kidney clinic in four weeks to check whether he is left with chronic kidney disease. The chart records each day’s decision, the triggers, and the family discussion of his goals of care.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Indications, not numbers. A high creatinine alone is a reason to write triggers, not to start.
  • Early starts did not save lives; very late starts may cost them. Decide each day.
  • Choose the modality the hospital can deliver. An unstable patient may be safer with slow therapy where he is.
  • Four lines in every order: indication, modality and why, who owns each task, and when to stop or transfer.
  • Look for recovery every day.
